title: When did the Fed’s response improve? A 150-year comparison of shocks and policy choices
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: Regis Barnichon and Geert Mesters find that the clearest improvement in US monetary policy came after the Volcker disinflation. Their comparison asks how much better policy could have performed given the disturbances each regime actually faced. A relatively low inflation or unemployment rate is an unreliable measure of policy quality when banking panics, energy shocks and changes in inflation expectations differ in size and frequency. In the authors’ estimates, the modern Fed did particularly well compared with its predecessors in responding to financial disturbances and supply-side shocks. The evidence ends in 2019. It gives no verdict on the subsequent inflation episode or on a particular serving chair.

They estimate responses of inflation, unemployment and the policy rate to policy and non-policy shocks. For a class of macroeconomic models these responses let them construct a feasible alternative rate path without specifying an entire structural model. They then measure two quantities. One is the adjustment to the observed reaction to a given shock, expressed relative to that reaction. The other is the reduction in the expected squared deviations of inflation and unemployment that the model says the best feasible response could have achieved. A large policy error need not produce a large aggregate loss if the shocks concerned are rare, small or relatively harmless. The counterfactual remains conditional on identifying comparable shocks and measuring policy transmission in each era.

The authors report average required path corrections greater than 100% in the gold-standard, early Fed and postwar periods, versus about 30% in absolute value in 1990–2019. They describe the modern corrections as statistically insignificant. The estimated consequences of mistakes differed markedly even among the earlier regimes. The table’s median overall distance to minimum loss is 97.4 for 1913–41, against 8.4 in 1879–1912, 6.6 after the Second World War and 3.2 in 1990–2019, on the study’s loss scale. The corresponding early Fed credible interval is wide, 57–230. These quantities are measures of model-implied avoidable macroeconomic loss. Applying them to GDP or converting them to yield basis points would change their meaning.

The bank-panic charts explain why the early Fed stands out. In the bottom row of the 1913–41 chart, the estimated policy rate rises in the early quarters of a financial shock even as inflation falls and unemployment rises. Real restraint intensifies just as activity needs support. In the adjusted response, the policy rate initially falls, unemployment rises less and the disinflation is much shallower. For 1990–2019 the estimated rate already falls after a financial shock. The adjusted and actual inflation responses are close, although the longer-run unemployment paths differ and uncertainty is substantial. Both panels extend to 20 quarters and use different vertical scales across periods. The similar heights of two plotted curves across charts therefore convey little about the relative economic size of a shock.

Postwar policy looks weak for a different reason. Following an inflation-expectations disturbance, the nominal rate initially responds too little to offset rising inflation. The authors infer that the resulting fall in the real rate reinforced the rise in prices. The adjusted response in the third chart raises the rate much more aggressively up front. Inflation subsequently peaks lower, at the cost of higher unemployment along much of the path. The result matters precisely because this is a trade-off. The model does not find that both inflation and unemployment could always have been lowered simultaneously. Energy and productivity disturbances also feature in the authors’ interpretation, although the postwar table interval for the productivity path correction crosses zero.

For someone choosing historical analogues, the implication is to match both the disturbance and the way policy reacted to it. The lower modern losses cannot, by themselves, establish that a pre-2008 or post-2008 training sample would generate better forecasts today. The modern estimate pools both, and the evaluation concerns a policy objective conditional on shocks. An out-of-sample forecast comparison requires a specified target, a forecast origin and data available at that origin. Nor do the estimates reveal a market price for a future intervention. They do explain why the same sign of a nominal rate movement can have very different implications when expectations or bank funding conditions move at the same time.

questions.question: Does the modern result survive separating the periods either side of 2008?
questions.detail: The 1990–2019 window spans both. A smaller average policy error could reflect genuinely improved responses or the composition of disturbances within that pooled period. Use the authors’ cited study and replication material to re-estimate comparable shocks and losses, report uncertainty in each short sample, and compare forecasts on a common later holdout.

questions.question: How robust is the historical ranking to the shock definitions and instruments?
questions.detail: Not every shock has an estimate in every era, and the interest-rate instrument and financial system changed. For a portfolio using banking crises as analogues, the distinction affects the expected timing of easing. Start with the identification and historical series in the cited paper, then test common shock definitions on overlapping samples.

questions.question: How sensitive is the postwar counterfactual to the weight on unemployment?
questions.detail: The plotted inflation improvement comes with greater unemployment after the expectations disturbance. The relative weight accorded to each deviation determines how much early tightening is judged desirable. Use the loss specification and alternative weights in a replication, comparing the whole path and its uncertainty before drawing conclusions about a supply shock today.

limitation: The post dates postwar coverage from 1954 in the prose and 1951 in the table and chart. The table note reverses the displayed panel descriptions, and the third chart’s note repeats the bank-panic wording despite its inflation-expectations heading. The analysis follows the displayed headers, plotted series and surrounding discussion.
